summary: The Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit gives corporations performing eligible R&D in Manitoba a 15% credit with no expenditure limit. This report provides a technical audit and legal analysis of the Research and Development (R&D) tax incentive architecture, statutory mechanics, administrative procedures, provincial regimes, and judicial precedents of Canada as of November 20261.

Canada’s flagship federal innovation incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program—underwent its most significant structural expansion in over a decade when Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 20261. Applicable retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and to depreciable property acquired or lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual cash refund on current expenditures from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue test ($15 million–$75 million), allowed Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) to elect into the gross revenue phase-out test, and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures, equipment lease costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) that had been repealed since 20141. Furthermore, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days4.

Practitioners and corporate claimants must navigate three critical compliance traps identified during this statutory audit. First, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for calculating notional SR&ED overhead under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations is 55% of the eligible salary base—not the outdated 65% rate that ceased to apply after 2012 or the 60% transitional rate from 20133. Second, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline—governed by subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of “investment tax credit” in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act (rather than the general six-year record-retention rule in paragraph 230(4)(b))—expires strictly 12 months after the corporation’s T2 filing due date (18 months after the corporate taxation year-end), with no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion under subsection 220(2.2) or subsection 220(3.1) to grant extensions for late-filed claims3. Third, provincial alignment with the federal Bill C-15 reforms is asymmetric: while British Columbia permanently aligned its provincial SR&ED credit with the $6 million limit and capital restoration, Ontario retained its $3 million Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) cap, Alberta maintained its independent $4 million Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), Saskatchewan implemented a province-specific $2 million refundable threshold, and Quebec replaced eight legacy innovation tax credits with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 20252.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Canadian SR&ED Regime

The Canadian SR&ED program is a federal tax incentive administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which executes technical, scientific, and financial administration7. Supporting 24,160 filed claims and $4.6 billion in allowed federal Investment Tax Credits in the CRA’s FY2025–2026 statistical period (April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026), the regime operates through a dual-incentive statutory mechanism embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (the “Act” or “ITA”) and the Income Tax Regulations (the “Regulations”)5.

The first statutory incentive is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the Act, which enables taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada to pool allowable current and (for acquisitions after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada20. A taxpayer may deduct any portion of this pool to reduce net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years21. The second statutory incentive is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under section 127 and section 127.1 of the Act, which provides a reduction of Part I federal income tax payable (at a basic rate of 15% or an enhanced rate of 35%) and, for qualifying corporations, a direct cash refund of unused credits3.

body.text: 1.2 The Bill C-15 Legislative Overhaul (Enacted March 26, 2026)

Following consultations by the Department of Finance, the federal government announced an initial package of SR&ED reforms in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled December 16, 2024), which originally proposed raising the enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million1. Subsequently, in Budget 2025 (Canada Strong, tabled November 4, 2025), the federal government expanded the proposed expenditure limit to $6 million while keeping the retroactive effective date for taxation years beginning after December 15, 20241. Both steps were enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 20261.

Any corporate tax advisory or financial statement analysis referencing a $3 million (or $4.5 million) expenditure limit, a $10 million–$50 million taxable capital phase-out, or the post-2013 exclusion of capital property for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, is outdated1. body.text: 1.3 Statutory Definition of SR&ED (Subsection 248(1)) and the “Why” and “How” Framework

Eligibility for SR&ED tax incentives is anchored in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which defines “scientific research and experimental development” as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis3. In August 2021, following program modernization efforts initiated in 2020, the CRA archived its 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and issued the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives40. While the statutory text of subsection 248(1) remained unchanged, the CRA structured its administrative guidance around two mandatory, interdependent requirements—the “Why” Requirement and the “How” Requirement40.

Under the “Why” Requirement (contained in paragraphs (a) to (c) of subsection 248(1)), work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement40. The CRA guidelines specify that this advancement must generate or discover conceptual knowledge (such as theories or prediction models) that advances the understanding of science or technology, rather than merely gathering factual knowledge (such as data or measurements)40. New knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists at the start of the project—meaning it is unknown or uncertain whether a given objective or result can be achieved due to an insufficiency in available scientific or technological knowledge40. Available knowledge comprises both the combined knowledge within the claimant’s business and sources reasonably available publicly40. Acquiring available knowledge or know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not constitute attempting to achieve a technological advancement40. Similarly, circumventing an uncertainty with a workaround using available knowledge fails the “Why” requirement3. However, achieving the original commercial or technical goal is not mandatory: learning through testing that a hypothesized solution is not viable still generates new knowledge40.

Under the “How” Requirement (contained in the opening words of subsection 248(1)), the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, performed by qualified individuals20. Merely taking a systematic approach or following established design methods, techniques, procedures, and standards is insufficient40. To satisfy the “How” requirement, the claimant’s work must include four steps40:

items: Defining a Problem: Observing and understanding the subject matter of the problem caused by the knowledge insufficiency43.
Advancing a Hypothesis: Generating an idea consistent with known facts (expressed as a possible solution, proposed method, or approach) toward resolving that problem23.
Planning and Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, where the hypothesis can evolve and change as a result of testing23.
Developing Logical Conclusions and Keeping Evidence: Formulating logical conclusions based on the experimental results and keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses40.

body.text: The Four Eligible Categories of Work (Paragraphs 248(1)(a) to (d))
Under subsection 248(1), work that satisfies the “Why” and “How” requirements must fall within one of four statutory categories12:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view (e.g., studying a newly discovered virus in a laboratory to better understand its characteristics)12.

Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view (e.g., developing a vaccine against a new virus by exploiting identified characteristics of that virus)40.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto (e.g., scaling up and optimizing processes for rapid, large-scale vaccine production)40. Experimental development is the most commonly claimed category of SR&ED work40. Characteristics indicating that existing technological knowledge is insufficient include: existing design methods are not applicable; requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; there are too many variables or unknowns; parameters or conditions are outside of the normal operating range; the nature of the problem is evolving; data is not readily available; or there are interlocking constraints40. While economic cost targets on their own do not create technological uncertainty, attempting to meet them may give rise to technological uncertainty40.

Paragraph 248(1)(d) — Support Work: Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer that is commensurate with the needs (matching in amount, size, extent, or duration) and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada31. Support work is not SR&ED on its own, and it must fall within one of eight statutory categories31:
Engineering40
Design40
Operations research40
Mathematical analysis40
Computer programming40
Data collection40
Testing40
Psychological research40

body.text: The Seven Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))
Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude seven categories of work from qualifying as SR&ED3:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion40.
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes40.
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities40.
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas40.
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process40.
Paragraph (j): Style changes40.
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection3.

body.text: As the CRA’s Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives emphasize, the key feature distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as “data collection” or “testing”) from excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) (“routine testing” or “routine data collection”) is purpose40. If data collection is carried out specifically to directly support scientific research or experimental development, it is eligible under paragraph (d); if it is performed as a routine activity to support normal business operations or quality assurance, it is excluded under paragraphs (f) and (k)40.
1.4 Geographic Nexus, Exclusive Economic Zone, and Foreign R&D Rules

To earn SR&ED ITCs and enter the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, SR&ED must generally be carried on in Canada and relate to a business of the taxpayer (or a related corporation under subsection 37(1.1)) carried on in Canada3. Under subsection 37(1.3), SR&ED performed in Canada’s exclusive economic zone is also included21.

When a Canadian taxpayer conducts or contracts for SR&ED outside Canada, two distinct statutory provisions govern the tax treatment. First, under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), a claimant may include permissible salary or wages paid to Canadian employees carrying on SR&ED outside Canada in its Canadian SR&ED claim, provided that the work performed outside Canada is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant, the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country, and the total claimed amount does not exceed the statutory cap calculated relative to total SR&ED salary and wages incurred in Canada under subsection 37(1.5)21. Second, under subsection 37(2) (Research outside Canada), all other current expenditures for SR&ED carried on outside Canada—including foreign contract payments and non-qualifying foreign wages—may be deducted when calculating current-year net income or loss for income tax purposes, but they cannot be included in the subsection 37(1) pool, cannot be claimed on Form T661, and earn no SR&ED ITCs3.
2. Rates, Expenditure Caps, Phase-Out Formulas, Refundability, and Carryovers

The financial value of an SR&ED claim depends on the claimant’s legal structure, corporate control status, prior-year size metrics, and whether the qualified expenditures are of a current or capital nature1.
2.1 Basic (15%) versus Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Rates

Under subsection 127(9) of the Act, the basic SR&ED ITC rate is 15% of the taxpayer’s “SR&ED qualified expenditure pool” at the end of the taxation year (the excess of qualified SR&ED expenditures over any provincial super-allowance benefit amount)9. Under subsection 127(10.1), an enhanced 20% ITC is added to the basic 15% rate—producing a combined enhanced ITC rate of 35%—on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation’s annual expenditure limit1.
For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, two classes of corporations qualify for the enhanced 35% rate up to the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit1:

items: Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs): Qualifying CCPCs throughout the taxation year1.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Extended by Bill C-15 under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) so that startups planning an Initial Public Offering (IPO) no longer automatically lose the enhanced 35% refundable rate upon listing1.

body.text: All qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a CCPC or ECPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit, as well as all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by other corporations, sole proprietorships (individuals), trusts, and partnerships, earn the basic 15% ITC rate3.
2.2 Phase-Out Mechanics for the $6 Million Expenditure Limit

Under Bill C-15, the maximum annual expenditure limit is $6,000,000 for both CCPCs (subsection 127(10.2)) and ECPCs (subsection 127(10.6)) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 20243. This $6 million limit begins to decrease once the corporation (together with its associated corporations or consolidated group) reaches $15,000,000 in size, and becomes nil ($0) at $75,000,000 or more1.
Method A: Prior-Year Taxable Capital Method (Default for CCPCs — Subsections 127(10.2) & 127(10.21))

Unless a CCPC elects to use the gross revenue method under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32), its expenditure limit is reduced based on the taxable capital employed in Canada for the previous taxation year (including all associated CCPCs)1. Under subsection 127(10.2), the initial threshold where the reduction begins is $15,000,000 (increased from $10,000,000 for tax years beginning before December 16, 2024) and the secondary threshold where the expenditure limit reaches nil is $75,000,000 (increased from $50,000,000 for tax years beginning before December 16, 2024)1.
Method B: Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Method (Mandatory for ECPCs under Subsection 127(10.6); Elective for CCPCs under Subsections 127(10.31) & 127(10.32))

Because an equity financing round can increase a CCPC’s taxable capital into the phase-out range even when commercial revenues remain low, and because public corporations are evaluated on revenue, Bill C-15 introduced a three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure1. Under subsection 127(10.6), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when the average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years (or the actual number of preceding fiscal years if the corporation has fewer than 3 fiscal years) reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) at $75,000,000 or more1.

items: Single Unassociated CCPC Election (Subsection 127(10.31)): Provides an annual election for an unassociated CCPC to have its expenditure limit determined under the subsection 127(10.6) revenue phase-out structure instead of the subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital formula8.
Associated CCPCs Election (Subsection 127(10.32)): Allows a group of associated CCPCs to elect to determine their shared expenditure limit using the revenue phase-out structure8.

Consolidated ECPCs (Subsection 127(10.62)): For an ECPC that is a member of a consolidated group preparing consolidated financial statements (as defined in subsection 233.8(1) in respect of an “ultimate parent entity” defined in subsection 127(9)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is shared among group members using the annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements8.

body.text: Short Taxation Years and Associated Corporation Allocations

If a corporation’s taxation year is less than 51 weeks, its expenditure limit must be prorated by multiplying the limit by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year divided by 3659. If an associated CCPC or consolidated ECPC has multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the expenditure limit for the subsequent taxation year in that calendar year equals the limit of the first taxation year, prorated if the subsequent taxation year is less than 51 weeks9. Associated CCPCs (determined under section 256 of the Act based on corporate control, regardless of activity) must allocate the shared $6 million expenditure limit among group members by filing Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026) under subsection 127(10.3); if they fail to file an agreement, the Minister may allocate the limit under subsection 127(10.4)3.
2.3 Refundability Rules Across Entity Types and Expenditure Categories

Under section 127.1 (Refundable Investment Tax Credit), specifically subsection 127.1(2) and amended subsection 127.1(2.01), the percentage of an unused SR&ED ITC that can be received as a cash refund (where no Part I tax is otherwise payable) depends on the claimant’s entity type, whether the credit was earned at the enhanced 35% rate or basic 15% rate, and whether the expenditure is of a current nature or a capital nature1.

Specifically, Bill C-15 amended subsection 127.1(2.01) (by adding elements A and B and redesignating paragraphs (a) and (b) as elements C and D) to establish that for both qualifying CCPCs and eligible ECPCs (that are neither qualifying corporations nor excluded corporations under subsection 127.1(2)), the enhanced 35% ITC is refundable at 100% for SR&ED expenditures of a current nature and 40% for SR&ED expenditures of a capital nature (for property acquired or lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024)1. Credits earned at the basic 15% rate by a qualifying corporation are refundable at 40%1. body.text: 2.4 Carryover Rules, Pool Adjustments, and Recapture of Investment Tax Credits
Carryback and Carryforward Periods

Unused SR&ED ITCs that are not deducted against Part I federal tax payable or refunded in the current taxation year may be carried back 3 years or carried forward up to 20 years under subsection 127(5) and subsection 127(9) to reduce Part I tax payable in those years3. Meanwhile, a positive balance in a taxpayer’s subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures does not expire and may be carried forward indefinitely to be deducted against business income in future taxation years21. Two statutory exceptions apply to the subsection 37(1) pool carryforward:

items: Partnerships (Paragraph 96(1)(e.1)): A partnership cannot carry forward a pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent taxation year; the entire pool must be deducted in calculating the partnership’s net income for tax purposes in the year incurred21. Furthermore, the portion of a partnership loss disallowed to a limited partner because it includes an SR&ED pool deduction is not allowed to other partners and does not become a limited partnership loss or non-capital loss24.

Loss Restriction Events (Paragraph 37(1)(h) and Subsection 37(6.1)): When corporate control of a corporation is acquired (or a trust has a new majority-interest beneficiary), the subsection 37(1) pool is reduced to nil unless the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, in which case deductions are restricted to income from that same or a similar business21.

body.text: Pool Reductions and Negative Pool Income Inclusion (Paragraphs 37(1)(e), 12(1)(t) & 12(1)(v))

Under paragraph 37(1)(e) and paragraph 12(1)(t), any federal SR&ED ITC deducted from Part I tax payable or refunded in a preceding taxation year (other than an ITC allocated from a partnership, which reduces the pool in the current year under subsection 127(12.1)) reduces the claimant’s subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures8. If decreases to the subsection 37(1) pool exceed increases at the end of a taxation year, the resulting negative pool balance must be brought into net income for tax purposes in that taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v), resetting the opening pool balance for the subsequent taxation year to nil (and any amount included in income under paragraph 12(1)(v) in a prior year is added back to the pool calculation under paragraph 37(1)(c.1))21.
Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Act and the CRA’s Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, a claimant’s SR&ED ITC will be recaptured (increasing Part I federal tax payable) if all four conditions in subsection 127(27) are met36:

items: The claimant acquired a particular property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (while paragraph 127(27)(a) refers to 10 preceding taxation years, subsection 127(36) extends this period to a maximum of 20 taxation years for ITCs earned in 1998 and subsequent taxation years)36;
The cost of the particular property was a qualified SR&ED expenditure36;

The cost of the particular property was included in an amount, a percentage of which can reasonably be considered to have been included in computing the claimant’s ITC at the end of the taxation year36; and

In the year, the claimant converts to commercial use or disposes of the particular property or another property that incorporates the particular property (including materials transformed in custom products, commercial assets, experimental production, or commercial production with experimental development; ASA capital equipment; Shared-Use Equipment; animals/growing things used in SR&ED; or property acquired through an SR&ED contract)36.

body.text: For standard property where no subsection 127(13) transfer occurred, the recapture amount added to Part I tax otherwise payable is the lesser of36:

items: Amount 1: The SR&ED ITC earned in respect of the particular property36; and
Amount 2: The historical ITC percentage rate used in calculating the SR&ED ITC earned on the property (35%, 15%, or 20% prior to 2014) multiplied by36:
The proceeds of disposition of the property (if disposed of to an arm’s length person)36; OR
The fair market value (FMV) of the property (if converted to commercial use or disposed of to a non-arm’s length party)36.

body.text: For Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under paragraph 127(27)(d), if both First Term and Second Term SUE were claimed, the recapture is the lesser of the total ITC obtained as First and Second Term SUE or the ITC calculated on 50% of the proceeds of disposition (or FMV)30. Where qualified expenditures were transferred to a non-arm’s length payer under subsection 127(13), the transfer itself does not trigger recapture if the intended use remains all or substantially all (ASA) for SR&ED, but subsection 127(29) requires recapture if the property is later sold or converted to commercial use36. All amounts added to tax payable under the recapture rules increase the claimant’s subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures for the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2) (or paragraph 37(1)(c.3) for partnership recapture excess)21.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Proxy vs. Traditional Methods, and Capital Rules
To claim SR&ED tax incentives, a taxpayer must link eligible technical work to allowable expenditures on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim)37.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged, Specified Employees, and YMPE Caps

Under subsection 248(1) and the CRA’s SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), “salary or wages” means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act4.

items: Amounts Included in SR&ED Salary or Wages: Regular salaries and wages incurred on or in respect of SR&ED (for employees “directly engaged” in hands-on SR&ED tasks under the Proxy Method, or employees “directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting” SR&ED under the Traditional Method); cash outlays for section 6 taxable benefits (and non-cash taxable benefits if a reasonable estimate of actual cost, excluding GST/HST/PST for which an input tax credit can be claimed, and not claimed elsewhere as a business expense); bonuses and remuneration based on profits for employees other than specified employees; and certain employment inducements or non-competition payments26.

Amounts Excluded from SR&ED Salary or Wages: Employer-paid related benefits (which may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method or covered by the PPA under the Proxy Method); extended vacation or sick leave (where the employee is not directly engaged/undertaking SR&ED); stock option benefits under section 7 (excluded under subsections 143.3(2), (3), and (5) as not being an expenditure); retiring allowances under subparagraph 56(1)(a)(ii) (not salary or wages by definition, though potentially allowable as overhead under the Traditional Method); and any salary or wages paid to a partner of a partnership (which the CRA treats as a distribution of partnership income)24.

All or Substantially All (ASA) Rule: Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) (Traditional Method) and subsection 2900(5) of the Regulations (Proxy Method), if all or substantially all (90% or more) of an employee’s duties are attributable to SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be claimed15.

180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4)): Salary or wages incurred in a taxation year but not paid within 180 days of the tax year-end are deemed not to have been incurred in that year (Line 315 of Form T661) and are excluded from both the subsection 37(1) pool and the ITC calculation20. When paid in a subsequent taxation year, they are entered on Line 310 of Form T661 for that year (though Line 310 amounts remain permanently excluded from the Proxy Method Salary Base under Regulation 2900(9))15.

body.text: Strict Rules for “Specified Employees” (Subsections 37(9)–(9.5) and Regulations 2900(7)–(8))

A “specified employee” (defined in subsection 248(1)) is an employee who does not deal at arm’s length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning directly or indirectly a significant share interest (10% or more of the issued shares of any class) in the corporation or a related corporation26. Specified employees are governed by three statutory restrictions:

items: Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): Bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to specified employees are strictly excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages26. CRA Commensurate Lump-Sum Exception: Under section 4.2 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, if an employee receives no salary throughout the year but receives a year-end lump-sum payment (otherwise structured as a bonus/profit share) that is commensurate with the SR&ED duties actually performed, the CRA may allow that amount as SR&ED salary or wages provided proper payroll deduction procedures are followed26.

Direct SR&ED Salary Cap (Subsections 37(9.1) to 37(9.5)): Subsections 37(9.1) through 37(9.5) impose a statutory cap on the direct SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee (limiting the salary or wages to 5 times the YMPE, prorated for the number of days on which the claimant is a specified employee during the year, under subsection 37(9.1), and requiring associated corporations to allocate this cap by filing an agreement under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.5), as set out in sections 6.1.1 and 6.1.2 of the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy)16.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Restrictions (Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8)): Under subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA’s Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the amount a claimant can include in the Salary Base (Part 5, Section A of Form T661) for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of3:

The 75% Rule: 75% of the specified employee’s total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior year’s unpaid salary or wages paid in the year on Line 310)3; OR

The 2.5 × YMPE Rule: 2.5 times the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) (determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan) for the calendar year in which the claimant’s taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days the individual was not a specified employee)3:

body.text: The cap is calculated as 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the tax year ends and B is the number of days in the tax year the claimant employed the individual15. Under subsection 2900(8) and subsection 2900(10), if a specified employee is employed by associated corporations (including deemed associated individuals or partnerships) with tax years ending in the same calendar year, the combined amount included in the Salary Base across all associated corporations cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE15.

Distinction Between YMPE and YAMPE: Although the Canada Pension Plan introduced a second earnings ceiling—the Year’s Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE)—starting in 2024 for CPP2 contributions, subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations references the first earnings ceiling (YMPE), not the YAMPE15. body.text: 3.3 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% Rate) and Overall PPA Cap (Regulations 2900(4) & 2900(6))

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA’s Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated in Part 5, Section B (Line 820) of Form T661 and entered on Line 502 at 55% of the Salary Base3:

items: Historical Rate Verification: The PPA rate was 65% up to 2012, 60% for 2013, and has been 55% since 20143. Using 65% on a current filing overstates the proxy amount by 10 percentage points and triggers audit adjustment3.

Salary Base Exclusions for All Employees (Regulation 2900(9)): For any employee (whether a specified employee or not), the Salary Base cannot include: (1) taxable benefits under section 6; (2) unpaid amounts from a prior year paid in the current year (Line 310 of Form T661); (3) remuneration based on profits; (4) bonuses; or (5) employer-paid related benefits15.

Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(6)): To ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed total business expenditures deducted in the year, subsection 2900(6) caps the PPA using the formula A − B − C15:

body.text: Where15:

items: A: Total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold)15;

B: Deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (e.g., CCA, interest, bad debts), Section 24 (cessation of business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), Section 37 (SR&ED expenditures), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts)15; and
C: Amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building15.

body.text: 3.4 Overhead, Cloud Computing, Materials, and Production Runs
Directly Related and Incremental Overhead (Traditional Method) and Cloud Computing

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Regulations, overhead and other current expenditures can only be claimed under the Traditional Method (Line 360 of Form T661) and must satisfy two tests25:

items: The Directly Related Test: The expenditure must have a direct linkage—with no intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED25.
The Incremental Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred3.

body.text: Cloud Computing Costs: Under these rules, cloud computing costs (such as elastic compute or storage instances used for R&D) are claimable only under the Traditional Method, provided the cost is directly related to SR&ED and incremental (would not have been incurred had the SR&ED work not been done)3. Under the Proxy Method, cloud computing costs cannot be claimed separately on Form T661 because the 55% PPA replaces overhead3.
Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Prototypes, and Production Runs

Under both the Traditional Method (paragraph 2900(2)(a)) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)), the cost of materials used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada is claimed on Form T661 under two categories20:

items: Materials Consumed (Line 320): Materials destroyed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of SR&ED (e.g., ink, chemicals, wood, or galvanized metal parts destroyed during testing)20. General utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas), cleaning supplies, broken lab supplies, CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants do not qualify as materials consumed (unless water is specifically identified, documented, and allocated as consumed in the SR&ED)38. Materials consumed are not subject to ITC recapture58.

Materials Transformed (Line 325): Materials modified, incorporated, or changed into another physical form, intermediate product, by-product, or final product as part of SR&ED that are not destroyed or rendered virtually valueless20. If transformed materials (or a custom product, commercial asset, prototype copy, or experimental production incorporating them) are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the ITC earned on the transformed materials is subject to recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36)36.

body.text: Pilot Plants, Prototypes, Custom Products, and Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP):

items: Pilot Plants vs. Commercial Plants (SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy): A pilot plant is a non-commercial facility used solely for SR&ED over its entire useful life; current expenditures (labour, materials, overhead) to develop and operate it qualify as SR&ED46. A facility intended for temporary or permanent conversion to commercial use is a commercial plant, where only isolated SR&ED work qualifies46. When apportioning costs in developing a custom product or commercial asset is difficult, claimants under either the Traditional or Proxy Method may use the Alternative Approach formula: the total actual costs of developing the custom product or commercial asset, minus the estimated costs that would usually be associated with constructing the asset had the technology already existed, plus an estimated amount representing the costs of materials transformed in SR&ED46.

Experimental Production (ED+EP) vs. Commercial Production (ED+CP) (SR&ED During Production Runs Policy): A production run is ED+EP when there is technical risk to the process or product from testing parameters outside normal tolerances and no simultaneous commercial work occurs; full labour, materials (excluding excess production beyond what is required for SR&ED), and overhead qualify47. A production run is ED+CP when SR&ED occurs simultaneously with commercial production without technical risk to regular output; only incremental labour, incremental material loss (actual loss minus standard loss), and incremental overhead qualify58. When isolating ED+CP expenses is impossible, the claimant may use the administrative Incremental Cost Method (actual run costs minus standard commercial production costs) only if the CRA agrees and the claimant signs a written waiver of the right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2) of the Act58.

body.text: 3.5 Subcontractors (80% Rule), Non-Arm’s Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments
Arm’s Length SR&ED Contracts (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and Subsection 127(9))

Under the CRA’s Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 27, 2026), when a claimant contracts an arm’s length taxable supplier to perform SR&ED on the claimant’s behalf in Canada28:

items: 100% of the allowable current contract expenditure is included in the subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Line 340 of Form T661)20; and

80% of the allowable contract expenditure qualifies for calculating the SR&ED ITC (with the 20% reduction entered on Line 529 of Form T661; payments to a non-taxable supplier are deducted on Line 528)3.

The Look-Through Rule (Subsections 37(14) and 37(15)): Under subsection 37(14), a claimant’s SR&ED contract expenditure must be reduced by any related expenditure of the performer that is not of a current nature, and under subsection 37(15), the performer must inform the claimant in writing of the reduction amount without delay if requested or no later than 90 days after the end of the calendar year in which the expenditure was made31.

Prepaid Expenses (Subsection 18(9)) and 180-Day Unpaid Amounts (Subsection 127(26)): Any payment for contracted SR&ED work not actually performed in the year is excluded as a prepaid expense under subsection 18(9)31. Any current expenditure (other than salary or wages) not paid within 180 days of the tax year-end remains in the subsection 37(1) deduction pool for the year incurred, but is deducted from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes on Line 520 of Form T66120. When paid in a subsequent year, it is claimed on Line 500 (“payment of prior years’ unpaid amounts (other than salary or wages)”), at 80% if it was an arm’s length contract expenditure20.

body.text: Non-Arm’s Length (NAL) Contracts (Subsections 37(13), 127(11.6), 127(13) & 127(24))

Under subsection 127(24), contract payments made to a non-arm’s length party for SR&ED do not qualify for an ITC in the hands of the payer unless the performer and payer file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm’s Length, updated May 15, 2026) under subsection 127(13)4. On Form T661, transferred qualified expenditures (which include the performer’s PPA) are reported on Line 508 by the transferee (payer) and deducted on Line 540 by the transferor (performer)4. Note that a partnership cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures on Form T1146 because a partnership is not a “person” or “taxpayer” for subsection 127(13) purposes24. Additionally, under subsection 127(11.6), non-arm’s length purchases of goods or services are restricted for ITC purposes to the cost incurred by the NAL supplier without any profit element30. Under subsection 37(13), in a non-arm’s length contract, expenditures for standalone support work (paragraph 248(1)(d)) can be claimed by the NAL performer when linked to SR&ED performed by the related payer26.
Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii) & (iii) and Form T1263)

Under the CRA’s Third-Party Payments Policy, a claimant may claim payments (Line 370 of Form T661, attaching Form T1263 for each payment) made to six types of entities (A Entity: Canadian resident corporation under 37(1)(a)(i.1); B Entity: approved association under 37(1)(a)(ii); C Entity: approved university, college, or research institute under 37(1)(a)(ii); D Entity: tax-exempt paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporation under 37(1)(a)(ii); E Entity: approved granting council under 37(1)(a)(ii); or F Entity: paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit corporation for basic/applied research under 37(1)(a)(iii)) for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the claimant’s business where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results20. Only 80% of a third-party payment qualifies for an ITC (20% reduced on Line 529)20. Payments to B–F entities are claimed on a cash basis in the year paid (exempt from prepaid expense rules under paragraph 18(9)(d)), whereas payments to A entities are claimed on an accrual basis in the year the SR&ED is performed32.
3.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and CCA Interaction

Under Bill C-15, capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs are eligible again for depreciable property acquired (or lease amounts first becoming payable) after December 15, 20241. Following Royal Assent, the CRA published the updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026)4.
1. SR&ED Capital Property (Paragraph 37(1)(b) and Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) & (B)(III))
To qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure22:

items: Timing and Ownership: The expenditure must be made after December 15, 2024, for depreciable property (expected useful life >12 months on which CCA could be claimed) that is owned (or held via leasehold interest) by the claimant and has become available for use (subsection 37(1.2))22.

Intended Use Standard (All or Substantially All — ASA ≥90%): At the time the expenditure is incurred, the property must be intended to be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, OR all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value must be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada3.

New vs. Used Property: Both new and used depreciable property meeting the criteria can be included in the subsection 37(1)(b) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, but used property (property used or acquired for use or lease for any purpose before acquisition by the claimant) is a prescribed expenditure under paragraph 2902(b) of the Regulations and is excluded from earning SR&ED ITCs22.

Exclusions: Land, leasehold interests in land, inventory, goodwill, and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings are excluded (with an exception for prescribed special-purpose buildings under section 2903 of the Regulations)3. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) is also excluded22.

Form T661 Reporting and CCA Interaction: Claimants must list the names of up to the 10 most expensive depreciable SR&ED properties acquired after December 15, 2024, on Line 262 of Form T661 and enter the percentage of total operating time for each property on Line 2634. Under subsection 37(6), an SR&ED capital expenditure deducted from income is deemed to be CCA allowed under paragraph 20(1)(a) and cannot also be depreciated on Schedule T2SCH83.

body.text: 2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) and Regulation 2900(11))

When new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, does not meet the ≥90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 (under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods) if it is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its actual operating time for SR&ED in Canada4:

items: First Term SUE (First Period): Measured from the date the property becomes available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time30. If actual SR&ED operating time is >50%, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowed money costs under section 21 and adjusted for NAL costs under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC30.

Second Term SUE (Second Period): Measured from the date the property became available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time30. If the property qualified as First Term SUE and cumulative actual SR&ED operating time over the Second Period is >50%, an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (totalling 50% of original capital cost across both terms)30.

Exclusions from SUE: SUE excludes used property, GPOEF, and Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) defined in subsection 2900(11) of the Regulations (property intended to be used in the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility, plant, or line under paragraph 2900(11)(c), or property intended at acquisition to be used over its expected useful life primarily for non-SR&ED purposes under paragraph 2900(11)(d))30. The capital cost of SUE is not included in the subsection 37(1) pool; it is depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH84.

body.text: 3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) & 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)/(VI))
For equipment lease costs incurred (first becoming payable) after December 15, 2024 (excluding building leases unless a prescribed special-purpose building approved by Finance Canada)8:

items: Traditional Method: If leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% is claimed as a lease cost35. If used less than 90% for SR&ED, the proportional percentage of SR&ED usage is claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures, provided the cost is directly related and incremental to SR&ED (including GPOEF)4.

Proxy Method: For leased equipment other than GPOEF, if used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed; if used more than 50% but less than 90% (primarily), 50% of the lease cost is claimed; if used 50% or less, 0% is claimed35. GPOEF lease costs are excluded under the Proxy Method4.

body.text: 4. Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) Classes and Immediate Expensing Rules
For capital property not claimed as an SR&ED capital expenditure under paragraph 37(1)(b), key CCA rules include3:

items: CCA Class 12 (100% Rate): Application software3.

CCA Class 50 (55% Base Rate; 100% Accelerated Deduction): Systems software and computer hardware3. Under Bill C-15, Class 50 property acquired after April 15, 2024, and available for use before 2027 receives a 100% first-year deduction3.
Half-Year Rule Suspension: Suspended at three times the normal first-year amount for eligible property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 20303.

Proposed Productivity Mega Deduction (Proposed September 15, 2026): On September 15, 2026, the federal government proposed allowing businesses to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of most depreciable property (covering roughly two-thirds of capital investment, excluding Class 1 buildings, goodwill, franchises, licences, and certain vehicles) acquired on or after September 15, 2026, once available for use10. As of autumn 2026, this measure remained proposed legislation10.

items: Statutory Basis: The expenditure filing deadline sits in subsection 37(11) of the Act, and the ITC filing deadline sits in paragraph (m) of the definition of “investment tax credit” in subsection 127(9)3. Both deadlines expire 12 months after the taxpayer’s income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year3.

Corporate 18-Month Window: Because a corporation’s T2 return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year under paragraph 150(1)(a), a corporation’s SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 18 months after the end of its taxation year (e.g., for a December 31, 2024 year-end, the deadline is June 30, 2026)3. Taxpayer relief under subsection 220(3.1) applies only to penalties and interest and cannot extend expired SR&ED claim windows3. A letter expressing an “intent to file” does not satisfy the statutory filing requirement59. body.text: 4.2 The New Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process introduced in Budget 2025, enabling eligible businesses to obtain an upfront determination of whether their planned projects qualify as SR&ED before starting work or incurring significant costs4.

items: Eligibility Criteria for Pre-Claim Approval: To qualify, the business and project must meet five cumulative conditions13:
The business must be a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership13;
The business must have an annual gross business income of less than $25,000,00013;
The business must be in good standing with the CRA13;
The project must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim (though projects where work has only recently begun may still apply)43; and
The project must not involve issues currently under litigation43.
Four-Step Application Workflow and Service Standards:
Step 1 — Request a Case Number: Complete the online web form (<5 minutes); the CRA issues a case number within 2 to 5 business days13.
Step 2 — Apply in My Business Account: Upload the application and existing project documentation in the CRA’s My Business Account portal for up to 3 projects13.

Step 3 — Meet with a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): Within 4 weeks of submission, an assigned RTA conducts a 2-to-5-hour meeting (virtual or on-site) to evaluate the existing state of technology, the scientific/technological uncertainty, and the planned systematic investigation13. This meeting is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and optional at the CRA’s discretion for existing claimants in good standing13.
Step 4 — Receive Determination Within 8 Weeks: Within 8 weeks of receiving the complete application, the RTA issues a written Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report4.

Validity and 90-Day Post-Filing Review Standard: If granted, Pre-Claim Approval is valid for up to 3 years (reported on Lines 212 and 214 of Form T661)4. When a refundable SR&ED claim containing only pre-approved projects is selected for an expenditure-only review, the CRA’s processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days (whereas claims with materially modified projects or non-pre-approved projects remain subject to the 180-day standard)13. There is no formal objection process if pre-claim approval is denied, but the RTA provides written reasons and the claimant may either re-submit a revised pre-claim application under a new case number or proceed to file a standard post-year-end Form T661 claim43.

4.4 The SR&ED Review Process, Escalation Steps, and Penalties

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025 and April 20, 2026), once an SR&ED claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn, as Form T661 and its certification form part of the signed income tax return4. Reviews are conducted (primarily virtually, or on-site on an exceptional basis) by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates technical eligibility and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who examines financial ledgers, vouchers, receipts, contracts, payroll tracking, and government assistance, reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM])14. Standard timelines for information requests are generally 30 days, and if adjustments are proposed in a Proposal Package, the claimant has 30 days to submit written representations before a final letter and Notice of Assessment or Reassessment are issued14.
The Four-Step Escalation and Dispute Resolution Process
Under the CRA’s Guidelines for resolving claimants’ SR&ED concerns, disputes follow four structured steps14:

items: Step 1 — Talk to the RTA and/or FR: Discuss eligibility or financial misunderstandings directly with the assigned reviewers before the file is closed14.

Step 2 — Contact the RTM and/or FRM: If unresolved, escalate to the Research and Technology Manager and/or Financial Review Manager, who reviews the facts and works with all parties to resolve concerns14.

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): If concerns remain after receiving the Proposal Package (and before the 30-day proposal period expires and before the file is closed), the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre, which forwards the request within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director14. An Administrative Review is not a second technical review; the Assistant Director evaluates strictly whether (1) the claimant was given due process and (2) the technical and financial reviews were consistent with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, resulting in a written letter of either Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered19.

Step 4 — Formal Notice of Objection and Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada: Within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant has the statutory right to file a formal Notice of Objection with the Appeals Branch of the CRA, and if still dissatisfied with the Appeals decision, to file an appeal with the Tax Court of Canada14.

items: Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty: Every claimant must complete Part 9 of Form T661 confirming whether a claim preparer was engaged (if no claim preparer assisted, only Lines 935, 970, and 975 are completed)4. If Part 9 claim preparer information is the only missing, incomplete, or inaccurate information, the SR&ED claim is not disallowed, but a $1,000 penalty may be assessed (referenced in CRA guidance alongside subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3))16.

Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2)): Under subsection 163(2) of the Act and the CRA’s Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission on an SR&ED claim, the civil penalty is the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of4:

Paragraph 163(2)(a): The understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (where taxable income in a loss year is deemed not to be less than zero under subsection 163(2.1), and overstated pool expenditures or overstated non-refundable ITCs are considered deducted first)27; PLUS

Paragraph 163(2)(d): The refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant27. Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of establishing on a balance of probabilities (more likely than not) that the false statement resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act; however, when the gross negligence penalty applies to a refundable ITC refund, the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refund regardless of what caused the overstatement27.

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive into Quebec’s 2025–2026 Innovation Overhaul: The CRIC and IDCI

In the Quebec Budget 2025–2026 (tabled March 25, 2025) and detailed further in the Quebec Budget 2026–2027 (tabled March 18, 2026), the Gouvernement du Québec introduced the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) as the central pillar of its new innovation tax assistance system, committing $2,412.6 million over five years (2025–2026 to 2029–2030) alongside $283.0 million over five years in Budget 2026–2027 for broader innovation ecosystem initiatives17.
1. Replacement of Eight Legacy Quebec Tax Measures

For corporate taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC replaced eight previously available tax measures (which could only be claimed for corporate taxation years beginning no later than March 25, 2025)17:

items: Four legacy R&D tax credits17;
Tax credit for an in-house design activity (industrial design component)17;
Tax credit for technological adaptation services17;
Tax holiday for foreign researchers17; and
Tax holiday for foreign experts17.

body.text: 2. Operational Parameters of the CRIC

items: Coverage of R&D and Pre-Commercialization Activities: Available to any corporation with an establishment in Quebec carrying on a business in Quebec, the CRIC supports both eligible R&D activities (basic research, applied research, and experimental development, where Quebec’s R&D definition is harmonized with the federal definition and the CRA conducts scientific reviews of the R&D work) and eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Quebec as a continuation of an R&D project carried out in Quebec by or on behalf of the corporation2. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include2:
Testing, technological validation, and studies required to obtain an initial regulatory approval or certification2;
Product design involving form, aesthetics, functionality, or material selection2; and
Certain quality control activities required for an initial approval or certification2.
Qualified Expenditures:
Labour costs (salaries and wages)17;
Equipment acquisition costs / equipment expenses17; and
50% of the amount of a subcontract entered into with an unrelated party, a university, a public research centre, or a research consortium17.
Exclusion Threshold: Eligible expenditures must exceed an annual Exclusion Threshold corresponding to the higher of17:
$50,000; OR

The basic personal amount under the personal income tax system applicable for each employee ($18,571 in 2025), adjusted according to the proportion of time the employee spent carrying out eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities17.

Fully Refundable Rates (30% and 20%): Rather than basing rates on company size, the CRIC provides a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures in excess of the exclusion threshold, and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on eligible expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 tier17.

body.text: 5.3 Canadian Patent Box Regimes: Quebec IDCI and Saskatchewan SCII
Two Canadian provinces operate statutory IP commercialization regimes offering reduced corporate income tax rates on qualifying IP revenues70:
1. Quebec Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI)

Applicable to taxation years beginning after December 31, 2020 (having replaced the former Deduction for Innovative Manufacturing Corporations [DIMC]), the IDCI (claimed on Form CO-737.18.CI) allows an eligible corporation with an establishment in Quebec to benefit from an effective tax rate of 2% on the qualified portion of its taxable income derived from the commercialization of a qualified intellectual property asset—a reduction of 9.5 percentage points from Quebec’s general corporate tax rate of 11.5%18.

items: Qualified IP Assets: Must be an incorporeal property resulting from R&D activities carried out in whole or in part in Quebec (which significantly contributed to its creation, development, or improvement) that is: (1) an invention protected by a patent or a certificate of supplementary protection; (2) software protected by copyright; or (3) a plant variety protected by a plant breeder’s rights certificate71.

Qualified Gross Income: Must be reasonably attributable to a Quebec establishment and consist of income from the sale or lease of property including the asset, income from supplying a service intrinsically related to the asset, royalties, or judicial damages relating to the asset71.

IDCI Calculation Elements: In simplified terms, the IDCI formula uses seven variables: A (net income for tax purposes), B (gross income from commercializing the IP asset), C (total gross income), D (estimate of profit not attributable to the IP asset), E (qualified amount of R&D expenditures related to the IP asset and Quebec), F (overall amount of R&D expenditures related to the IP asset), and G (the factor (11.5% − 2%) ÷ 11.5%, written as 0.826% in the government web summary)71.

body.text: 2. Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII)

Introduced in the 2017–2018 Saskatchewan budget and open for applications until June 30, 2027, the SCII offers eligible corporations commercializing qualifying intellectual property a reduction of the provincial Corporate Income Tax (CIT) rate from the standard 12% to 6% (on qualifying income above the $600,000 small business rate threshold) for a period of 10 years or 15 years depending on where the research and development takes place, with no annual cap on savings68.
6. Stacking Mechanics: Government Assistance, Federal Grants, and Clean Economy ITCs
6.1 Statutory Mechanics of “Government Assistance” and “Contract Payments”

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(11.1), 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, as detailed in the CRA’s Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, any government assistance, non-government assistance (amounts included under paragraph 12(1)(x)), or contract payment in respect of SR&ED that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its filing-due date reduces its qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar (Lines 513 to 517 of Form T661)3.

items: Government Assistance Scope (Subsection 127(9)): Includes grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, deductions from tax, or investment allowances from any government, municipality, or public authority—including provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself)28. While bona fide concessional loans with reasonable repayment terms from public authorities are excluded from the definition of “government assistance,” any loan whose repayment is contingent on future profits/revenues (such as royalties) or subject to a forgiveness ceiling is treated by the CRA as government assistance28.

Project-by-Project Floor and PPA Exception: Assistance for a specific project reduces only that project’s deductible expenditures in the subsection 37(1) pool down to nil; any excess assistance over the project’s expenditures is included in income28. Furthermore, under the Proxy Method, the portion of government or non-government assistance (such as a provincial tax credit) that relates to the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) reduces qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(18), but does not reduce the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, it is included directly in income for the taxation year it is received under paragraph 12(1)(x)28.

body.text: 6.2 Worked Numerical Stacking Examples (Provincial Credits and NRC IRAP)
Worked Example 1: Ontario Qualifying CCPC Combining OITC, ORDTC, and Federal SR&ED

As documented in practitioner analyses of Ontario and federal credit interactions, because Ontario R&D credits are government assistance under subsection 127(18) that reduce the federal qualified expenditure base, combining provincial and federal credits is sequential rather than simple additive arithmetic50. For a qualifying CCPC in Ontario claiming the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount on $1,000,000 of eligible direct SR&ED salaries50:

items: Gross Qualified Expenditures (Including 55% PPA): $1,000,000 direct salary + $550,000 PPA (55%) = $1,550,00015.
Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — 8% Refundable on Schedule 566): $1,550,000 × 8% = $124,000 in cash2.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — 3.5% Non-Refundable on Schedule 508): Computed on the expenditure base net of OITC ($1,550,000 − $124,000 = $1,426,000 × 3.5% = $49,910 non-refundable; or the corporation may waive the ORDTC under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) if it has no Ontario tax payable and wishes to prevent the non-refundable credit from reducing its 35% cash-refundable federal credit)50.
Federal Enhanced 35% Refundable ITC (Schedule T2SCH31):

If the ORDTC is waived, the net federal qualified expenditure base is $1,550,000 − $124,000 = $1,426,000, yielding a 35% federal cash refund of $499,100 and a combined immediate cash return of $124,000 + $499,100 = $623,100 (62.31% of direct SR&ED salary in cash)9.

If the ORDTC is claimed, the net federal qualified expenditure base is $1,550,000 − $124,000 − $49,910 = $1,376,090, yielding a 35% federal cash refund of $481,631.50 and a total combined credit return of $124,000 + $49,910 + $481,631.50 = $655,541.50 (65.55% of direct SR&ED salary, matching the ~62% to 66% combined return range)9.

body.text: Worked Example 2: Stacking NRC IRAP Grant (80% Labour Coverage) with Federal SR&ED

Under subsection 127(18) and the Proxy Method rules in subsection 2900(4), when an SME receives an NRC IRAP grant covering 80% of a $100,000 eligible R&D salary ($80,000 grant), the $80,000 grant reduces the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool15:

items: If calculated strictly on the out-of-pocket salary before proxy ($100,000 − $80,000 = $20,000 net salary expenditure), the out-of-pocket salary portion is $20,00077.

Furthermore, because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount ($55,000) on Form T661 (Part 5) is computed on the $100,000 directly engaged salary base before deducting government assistance on Line 515 ($100,000 salary + $55,000 PPA − $80,000 IRAP assistance = $75,000 net qualified expenditures), a qualifying CCPC earns a 35% federal ITC of $26,250 on top of the $80,000 IRAP grant15.

body.text: 6.3 Major Federal Innovation Grants and Co-Funding Programs
Key federal direct funding programs that interact with SR&ED (subject to a 75% total government assistance stacking limit across federal, provincial, and municipal sources) include77:

Budget & Reach: Operates an annual budget of $437 million across 4 active programs supporting approximately 3,100 incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs (≤500 FTE employees) per year77. (On December 19, 2023, the Government of Canada announced that full implementation of the Canada Innovation Corporation [CIC] will occur no later than 2026–2027, until which time NRC IRAP remains under the NRC77.)

Typical awards range from $75,000 to $1,000,000 (median award $75,000, average grant $94,000, per-firm average $168,000, and major project ceiling up to $10,000,000)77. Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) / Strategic Response Fund (ISED):
Administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) for large-scale innovation projects with eligible project costs starting at $10,000,000+77.
NSERC Alliance Grants & Mitacs:

NSERC Alliance Quantum Grants — SME Partner Stream: Provides $100,000 to $650,000 per year for up to 2 years (typical total project funding of $500,000 to $900,000) for university-led quantum research partnerships advancing the National Quantum Strategy, requiring completion of the Tri-agency Policy on Sensitive Technology Research and Affiliations of Concern (STRAC) attestation form77. body.text: 6.4 Interaction with Federal Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits (Sections 127.44 to 127.491)

Canada’s five refundable Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits (Sections 127.44, 127.45, 127.48, 127.49, and 127.491 of the Income Tax Act) are aggregated alongside SR&ED on Schedule 31 (T2SCH31) of the T2 corporate return44:

items: Clean Technology ITC (Section 127.45 — Schedule 75 & T2SCH31 Line 155): Enacted via Bill C-59 in 2024, providing a 30% refundable tax credit (with no expenditure cap) on the capital cost of new qualifying property drawn from CCA Classes 43.1, 43.2, and 56 (wind, solar, small hydro, stationary battery/pumped hydro electricity storage, low-carbon heat pumps/geothermal, concentrated solar, non-road zero-emission industrial vehicles and charging, small modular nuclear reactors [SMRs], and waste biomass electricity/heat) that becomes available for use between March 28, 2023, and December 31, 2033, dropping to 15% in 2034 and 0% after 2034 (with a November 5, 2026 proposal to extend eligibility to before 2041)44. To receive the full 30% rate (rather than the 20% reduced rate), claimants must elect and attest on Schedule 75 and Schedule 31 to meeting prevailing union wage and 10% Red Seal apprenticeship hour labour requirements44.

Clean Tech Manufacturing ITC (Section 127.49): A 30% refundable tax credit for capital investments in equipment used to manufacture or process clean technology (beginning to phase down in 2032), mutually exclusive on a property-by-property basis with the Clean Tech ITC44.

Clean Hydrogen ITC (Section 127.48): A 15% to 40% refundable tax credit for hydrogen production equipment depending on carbon intensity (highest rate under 0.75 kg CO2 / kg H2; 0% at 4 kg CO2 / kg H2 or higher), subject to the prevailing wage and apprenticeship labour requirements44.

Clean Electricity ITC (Section 127.491): A 15% credit primarily available to provincial Crown utilities, pension funds, and certain Indigenous corporations; cannot be stacked on the same property as the Clean Tech ITC44.
Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) ITC (Section 127.44): Refundable ITC for eligible CCUS equipment, subject to prevailing wage and apprenticeship labour requirements44.

body.text: While the same capital asset cannot be double-claimed under multiple Clean Economy ITCs or SR&ED, cleantech companies routinely combine SR&ED (for the R&D work that develops the clean technology) with the Clean Tech ITC or Clean Tech Manufacturing ITC (for the capital deployment or manufacturing equipment)44.
7. Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Tax Court of Canada Precedents
7.1 The Foundational Five-Question Judicial Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998)

The foundational judicial authority interpreting the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) is the decision of Judge Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (Tax Court of Canada), which was formally adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (para. 17)41. Even after the CRA introduced its simplified two-requirement (“Why” and “How”) administrative guidelines in August 2021, both the five questions and the two requirements derive from the unchanged text of subsection 248(1), and the Tax Court of Canada continues to adjudicate SR&ED appeals using the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria41:

items: Question 1 (Technological Risk or Uncertainty): Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?45

Question 2 (Formulation of Hypotheses): Did the person claiming SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? (This involves observing the subject matter of the problem and formulating an idea consistent with known facts as a starting point for further investigation)45.

Question 3 (Scientific Method / Systematic Investigation): Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method (or systematic investigation or search), including trained observation, measurement/experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?45

Question 4 (Technological Advancement): Did the process result in a technological advancement (or was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement)?45
Question 5 (Contemporaneous Record-Keeping): Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?45
